title: WIP, FO, SAL, Frog and Other Cross Stitch Terms: A Beginner Glossary

seo.title: WIP, FO, SAL, Frog and Other Cross Stitch Terms: A Beginner Glossary
seo.meta_description: Beginner cross stitch glossary explaining WIP, FO, FFO, SAL, frog, UFO, ORT, confetti, parking, stash and other common community terms.
seo.search_intent: Beginners who see abbreviations and jargon such as WIP, FO, FFO, SAL, frog, UFO and ORT in cross stitch communities and want clear definitions.

excerpt: Understand the abbreviations and expressions that appear constantly in cross stitch groups, forums and videos.
content_html:
When you first enter cross stitch groups, videos or forums, abbreviations such as WIP, FO, FFO, SAL, UFO, ORT and frog can make ordinary conversations look surprisingly technical. Most of these terms do not describe difficult techniques. They are simply shortcuts the community uses when talking about projects, progress and supplies.

You do not need to memorize the vocabulary before you stitch. This glossary covers the terms that appear most often so you can recognize them when they show up in a post, pattern discussion or project update.

WIP, FO, FFO and UFO describe project status

WIP means work in progress: a project that has been started but is not finished. If someone says they have five WIPs, they have five active or partially active stitching projects.

FO usually means finished object. In cross stitch, it often describes a piece where the stitching itself is complete even if washing, pressing, framing or sewing still remains.

FFO means fully finished object. The embroidery has been completed and turned into its final form, such as framed art, a cushion, ornament or card.

UFO means unfinished object. It often refers to a project that has been put away for a long time or effectively abandoned. A project can move from active WIP to UFO and back again.

SAL and other terms for shared or rotating projects

SAL means stitch along. Multiple stitchers work on the same project or theme according to a shared schedule. Sometimes the whole pattern is known from the beginning; other SALs release the design in installments.

A mystery or installment SAL may publish one section each week or month. Much of the appeal comes from stitching at the same pace as other people and comparing different fabric and color choices.

You may also see start for a newly begun project, finish for a completed piece and rotation for a system where someone alternates among several WIPs on a schedule.

Frog and frogging mean removing stitches

Frog or frogging refers to taking stitches out. The common explanation is the wordplay “rip it, rip it,” echoing the sound associated with a frog. If someone says they had to frog a section, they removed stitching to correct a mistake.

Not every mistake requires frogging. One isolated stitch in a very similar shade may never be noticed, while an entire row placed one square off can affect everything that follows and is usually worth correcting.

You may also see people discuss stitching over, compensating for or leaving an error. Those choices depend on how visible the mistake is and whether the correction would create extra thickness or distort nearby stitches.

ORT, floss toss, stash and other supply terms

ORT is commonly used for the tiny thread ends cut away while stitching. Some stitchers collect them in a jar as a visual record of one project or a whole year.

Floss toss means laying the proposed threads on top of the chosen fabric to see how the colors work together before stitching. It is especially useful with dark, dyed or unusual fabric.

Stash is your personal collection of supplies: floss, fabric, patterns, needles and accessories. “Shopping the stash” means using materials you already own instead of buying new ones.

A kit contains a pattern plus some or all of the required materials. Kitting up means gathering the fabric, floss and tools needed to start a particular chart.

Confetti, parking and cross-country describe chart or stitching behavior

Confetti describes areas containing many isolated stitches of different colors. It is not a special stitch; it is a chart characteristic that often slows progress.

Parking is a method where several colors remain threaded or positioned near the next place they will be used. It is common in large or full-coverage designs.

Cross-country usually means following one color across a section before changing to another, moving through the chart wherever that shade appears.

Full coverage means nearly the entire design area is filled with stitches. Monochrome describes a chart worked in one color or a very restricted color family.

Not every community uses the jargon in exactly the same way

The boundaries between terms can vary. FO and FFO, for example, are not always separated consistently. Some stitchers simply call the stitching a finish even before it is framed.

You will also encounter names of methods, apps and tools that look like jargon. If a term describes a specific technique—parking, railroading or loop start—it is usually more useful to learn the technique itself than memorize a one-line definition.

Context often solves the problem. “My new WIP,” “I had to frog this section” and “I joined a SAL” make the meaning fairly clear once you know the basic vocabulary.

Cross stitch jargon exists to make community conversations quicker, not to create a barrier for beginners. Understanding WIP, FO, FFO, SAL, frog, UFO, ORT, stash and confetti will already make a large share of common posts easy to follow, and the rest becomes familiar naturally as you stitch.
